title: South Africa holds by one vote as transport drives 40% of inflation and core prices trend up
summary: South Africa’s Monetary Policy Committee held the rate at 7.25% on 19 November. Four members preferred no change, while three wanted a 25 basis point increase. After two adjustments during 2026, the majority judged a moderately restrictive stance sufficient for now; the committee explicitly retained scope to tighten further. The split matters because the projected decline in headline inflation depended heavily on the comparison base for fuel. A fall in annual inflation as unusually low pre-war fuel prices leave the twelve-month window could help inflation return towards 3% without establishing that service providers and other firms had aligned their future price-setting with target.

The magnitude of the fuel shock was already observable. In Gauteng a litre of unleaded 93 petrol cost R29.87 in November, compared with R20.97 a year before. The fuel component accounts for 3.8% of CPI and the broader transport category for 13.89%. In October, transport contributed 2.1 percentage points to headline inflation of 5.2%, just over 40% of the total. Contribution and basket weight answer different questions: an unusually fast price increase can make a category responsible for a much larger share of current inflation than its normal expenditure share. The Bank projected fuel inflation of 39% in Q4 2026, 33.2% in Q1 2027 and minus 3.4% in Q2 2027. That reversal is an annual comparison and does not require petrol to return to its old nominal price (statement p. 2, footnotes 6–8).

Core inflation complicated the case for waiting. The Bank forecast core inflation averaging 3.8% in 2026 and 4.0% in 2027 even as headline inflation fell from 4.3% to 4.0% on those same annual averages. Core goods had benefited from a stronger rand and were expected to rise from 1.7% inflation this year to 3.8% next year. Food prices could also become less favourable as weather and fuel costs changed. Market-based inflation expectations had eased modestly since September, but there was little new surveyed evidence. The forecast itself assumed a decline in the BER two-year measure from 3.9% in Q3 2026 to 3.4% in Q4 2027. That future survey path is a conditioning mechanism, not an observed re-anchoring. The Bank explicitly wanted to see the upward core trend reverse (pp. 3–4).

The growth baseline remained modest, but its composition had changed. GDP revisions altered the level of output more than recent growth rates, and the second-quarter contraction remained. Wholesale and retail sales pointed to a recovery in household demand. The consumption forecast for 2026 rose from 2.1% to 2.7%, while fixed investment was revised from minus 0.1% to minus 0.3%. The investment share of output, roughly 13%, also reflected the rebase of the national accounts. The Bank saw downside growth risks and doubted that a consumption-led recovery alone would sustain higher medium-term growth. The forecast annex kept real GDP growth at 1.2% for 2026 and 1.7% for 2027. A similar aggregate growth path thus masked a material revision to which borrowers and industries were generating demand.

Two conditional scenarios map different shocks into South African assets. With oil peaking at US$130 and refinery margins elevated, 2027 inflation reached 5.4% against a 4.0% baseline, growth fell to 1.3% against 1.7%, and the model policy rate peaked at 7.73%. A global fiscal-risk scenario raised foreign bond yields and South Africa’s risk premium while weakening the rand. It produced 5.6% inflation, 1.2% growth and a rate peak of 7.84%. Their similar policy implications conceal a valuable distinction: the energy case starts with the local-currency price of fuel, while the fiscal case reprices sovereign credit and the currency. Neither scenario was assigned a probability or identified as the reason for a particular dissent (pp. 4–5, footnotes 16–17).

The baseline QPM rate path averaged 7.15% in Q4 2026, 6.89% in Q1 2027 and 6.57% in Q3. Its later easing depends on inflation falling back towards target; it is neither the announced 7.25% spot rate nor a sequence of future votes. The press statement’s footnotes give two slightly different Q4 2027 headline estimates, 3.3% in footnote 10 and 3.2% in footnote 19. The accompanying Forecast Report’s quarterly results table (p. 3) gives 3.3% for Q4 2027 and 4.0% for the full year. Its policy-rate fan chart (p. 6) widens as the horizon lengthens. The symmetric bands combine historical forecasting experience and model simulations, so they do not express the committee’s assessment that inflation risks lean upwards. A model path back towards neutral can therefore coexist with three members preferring an immediate increase. Determining the surprise for bondholders would require the price of that outcome before the vote.

questions.question: Can underlying prices turn down while fuel base effects lower headline inflation?
questions.detail: Reconstruct the transport and fuel contributions using their different basket weights, then compare the rest of goods and services with unit labour costs and survey expectations. The question matters because the model assumes that expected inflation will move closer to target. A mechanical decline in headline inflation with continued broad core increases would offer weaker grounds for later easing.

questions.question: Which adverse scenario better fits changes in the rand and South African bond yields?
questions.detail: Examine oil, refinery margins, shipping costs, global sovereign yields and domestic sovereign spreads in comparable windows. Look for movement in inflation-linked pricing and the currency, with controls for common dollar news. Energy and fiscal risks both produce higher inflation and weaker output in the model, but their first observable market signals and the sectors bearing their costs differ.

questions.question: Did the narrow vote push out the market-implied date of the first cut?
questions.detail: Compare pre- and post-announcement rates spanning individual meetings, then examine later forwards and international yields. A held policy rate can still deliver a meaningful path surprise when three members preferred a hike. The forecast’s Q4 average and the committee’s current overnight rate are different measures; neither establishes the expected decision already in market prices.
